claims.text: The protoconch is the embryonic or larval shell of a gastropod; the rest of the shell grows on from it, and in some species it dissolves once the juvenile shell starts forming.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The aperture is the main opening of the shell. The shell grows by thin layers added to the aperture's edge from the mantle border, the main agent in making shell.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The soft body is held in the shell by the columellar muscle, attached along the columella. Contracting it pulls the foot, head and other soft parts into the shell, away from predators and drying out, and draws the operculum against the opening.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The operculum sits on the upper surface of the foot and acts as a trapdoor that closes the opening when the animal withdraws. Its most essential function is to stop the snail drying out; where it seals fully it also protects against predators.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The inhalant siphon is a tube-like extension of the mantle that draws water into the mantle cavity and over the gill for breathing. It carries chemoreceptors that "smell" or "taste" the water to hunt for food.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The mantle is the body wall that covers the visceral mass. Its skin secretes calcium carbonate and conchiolin to build the shell. In cowries the living animal often partly or fully covers its glossy shell with the mantle.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: Gastropods typically have a well-defined head with two or four sensory tentacles bearing eyes, and a foot positioned below the guts, which gives them their name ("stomach-foot"); like most molluscs they move on this single muscular foot. Many smell through receptors in the skin of their tentacles.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The queen conch has a long snout, two eyestalks with well-developed eyes, extra sensory tentacles, a strong foot and a sickle-shaped operculum. It browses algae and plant material in seagrass beds and scavenges decaying plant matter.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The queen conch moves by leaping: it digs the point of its sickle-shaped operculum into the sand, then extends the foot and throws the shell forward. Only the front third of the foot touches the ground, and leaping may stop predators following a continuous scent trail.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The flared lip is absent in juveniles and grows once the conch reaches reproductive age; the thicker the lip, the older the conch. Its body's visceral hump stays inside the shell and holds the internal organs.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: The siphuncle empties water from new chambers as the shell grows: the animal makes the blood in it saltier, water leaves the chamber by osmosis, and gases diffuse in. It is passive, not pumping.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: A nautilus has 50 to over 90 tentacles of three kinds. Ocular tentacles beside the eyes are sensory; digital and labial tentacles ring the mouth. They have no suckers, yet the digital tentacles grip with an adhesive from ridges on their surface and let go by contracting.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: To swim, a nautilus draws water into and out of its living chamber with its funnel (hyponome), by jet propulsion, which has proved efficient compared with other jet-propelled animals like squid and jellyfish.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: A hermit crab's abdomen is soft and not hardened by calcium, so it must occupy a shell made by another animal or be defenceless; almost 800 species carry such mobile shelters, most often snail shells.
claims.evidenceNote: Read for what the part does. Applies to the group named in the claim; species-specific details cite their own source.

claims.text: Moon snails (naticids) plough through sand hunting bivalves and other prey, leaving countersunk bore-holes in the shells they drill.

claims.text: The radula, often compared to a tongue, is a ribbon of tiny teeth that scrapes or cuts food before it is swallowed.
